paragraphs: Keyphrases give readers a compact description of a document’s main topics. Research on producing them automatically has concentrated on English, partly because suitable training datasets for other languages are scarce. This paper addresses that gap with Papyrus, a collection of 16,427 abstract–keyphrase pairs intended to support multilingual keyphrase research.

The authors release four versions that separate different language requirements. Papyrus-e targets English keyphrases, while Papyrus-f targets French. Papyrus-m allows keyphrases in any language, predominantly French and English, and Papyrus-a targets keyphrases in several languages. These versions make it possible to study related but distinct tasks rather than treating multilingual output as one uniform problem.

Training a state-of-the-art model on these tasks improves non-English results, with reported average gains of 14.2% for extraction and 2.0% for generation. Combining Papyrus-e with the Kp20K training set also improves English results by 0.4% and 0.7%, respectively. The contribution is therefore both a resource for understudied languages and evidence that its English portion can complement an existing training collection.
neurips-2022-a-new-dataset-for-multiling.tldr: Papyrus supplies multilingual abstract–keyphrase pairs and improves reported keyphrase extraction and generation results.

paragraphs: A randomized experiment can give biased conclusions when treating one unit changes another unit’s outcome. This paper studies a particular network structure: treatments and outcomes belong to units on one side of a bipartite graph, while connections through units on the other side transmit interference. Such indirect interactions arise in marketplaces and two-sided platforms.

The authors formalize this setting using exposure mappings, which describe how treatment assignments translate into the treatment conditions a unit experiences. They identify situations where existing methods for assigning whole clusters to treatment fail to adequately control interference. They then derive a balanced graph-partitioning objective by minimizing the bias of the difference between treatment and control means.

Under their model, the resulting design is minimax optimal within a class of linear potential-outcome models with bounded interference. This is a worst-case guarantee within that specified class, rather than across every possible outcome mechanism. The paper also supplies theoretical and experimental evidence that the design remains robust across varied interference graphs and outcome models.
neurips-2022-cluster-randomized-designs-.tldr: A balanced clustering objective yields experimental designs that control indirect interference and have a specified minimax optimality guarantee.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic variational inequalities when information is spread across many devices and differs between them. The setting permits unbounded domains and heterogeneous, non-identically distributed data. Its network assumptions accommodate both decentralized communication with changing connections and centralized arrangements used in federated learning.

The authors extend the stochastic extragradient method so workers can perform multiple local updates between communications. This provides a way to reduce communication frequency while retaining a framework for analyzing convergence. Their rates explicitly track network properties such as mixing time, as well as data heterogeneity, stochastic variance, the number of devices, and the number of iterations.

The analysis covers strongly monotone and monotone problems, along with non-monotone problems when a Minty solution exists. That additional condition matters for interpreting the non-monotone result. Distributed stochastic saddle-point problems are included as a special case, connecting the framework to generative adversarial network training. Experiments on decentralized GAN training demonstrate the proposed method’s effectiveness in a setting described as particularly challenging.
neurips-2022-decentralized-local-stochas.tldr: An extended stochastic extragradient method supports heterogeneous distributed optimization with local updates and convergence guarantees for several problem classes.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality images, but producing an image usually involves a long sequence of sampling steps. That sequence creates two difficulties: sampling takes time, and propagating gradients through it is cumbersome. The latter matters for model inversion, where the goal is to find a latent noise input that approximately reproduces a known image.

The paper extends denoising diffusion implicit models by representing the entire sampling trajectory as one joint fixed-point system. In this formulation, the states along the trajectory must satisfy a collection of mutually consistent relationships. Viewing the chain as a deep equilibrium model allows a parallel sampling approach in place of the usual fully serial process.

The same formulation supplies fast gradients for finding noise inputs during inversion. The authors report strong results on CIFAR10, CelebA, and LSUN Bedroom and Churches. They also describe the approach as complementary to other sampling and inversion improvements. Its central contribution is thus a different computational organization of diffusion sampling that benefits both image generation and recovering an image’s generating noise.
neurips-2022-deep-equilibrium-approaches.tldr: Recasting a diffusion sampling chain as a joint equilibrium system enables parallel sampling and faster model inversion.

paragraphs: Pairwise comparisons provide observations about which of two items is preferred or wins, while the Bradley–Terry–Luce model combines those observations into a global ranking. When comparisons arrive over time, a single fixed ranking may no longer describe the data. This paper asks how to locate the times when the underlying ranking changes abruptly.

The analysis uses a high-dimensional model whose parameters are piecewise constant: they remain fixed within each time segment and change at unknown boundaries. The authors develop practical algorithms based on dynamic programming to estimate those boundaries. This makes the timing of changes an explicit inference target, rather than forcing one ranking to summarize the entire sequence.

The paper establishes consistency and gives rates that explicitly depend on model parameters, the spacing between successive changes, and the size of each change. These dependencies connect estimation accuracy to the structure of the changing process. Extensive numerical experiments and a real-life example support the theoretical findings, grounding the proposed change-localization methods in both controlled and applied settings.
neurips-2022-detecting-abrupt-changes-in.tldr: Dynamic-programming algorithms consistently locate abrupt ranking changes in a piecewise-constant Bradley–Terry–Luce model.

paragraphs: Cross-device federated learning trains a shared model using data that stays on individual devices. Evaluating this approach requires datasets that reflect differences between users as well as the scale of the participating population. The paper introduces FLAIR because existing image benchmarks do not adequately capture these properties for many real-world uses.

FLAIR contains 429,078 images contributed by 51,414 Flickr users and supports multi-label classification, where one image can have several labels. Its user-associated data captures heterogeneity across people, while its long-tailed label distribution means that some labels are much more common than others. These properties make the dataset relevant to challenges that arise when learning across diverse user data.

The authors implement several baselines across different learning setups and tasks, providing reference points for subsequent work. The dataset and benchmark code are available together. The paper’s main contribution is a large, annotated evaluation resource: it creates opportunities to compare federated learning methods under challenging user and label distributions, rather than presenting a single new training algorithm.
neurips-2022-flair-federated-learning-an.tldr: FLAIR provides a large image benchmark with diverse user data and uneven label frequencies for federated learning research.

paragraphs: This paper isolates the effect of a single training step on the features of a randomly initialized two-layer neural network. The first-layer weights receive one gradient update using mean squared error, after which ridge regression is analyzed on the resulting features. This separates the value of changing the representation from the effects of a long training process.

The theory assumes an idealized student–teacher problem with a single-index teacher, while sample size, input dimension, and network width grow proportionally. For a small first-step learning rate, the authors establish a Gaussian equivalence property. The updated representation improves on the initial random features, but its prediction performance cannot surpass that of the best linear model on the original input.

With a sufficiently large learning rate, the conclusion changes for certain teacher functions: ridge regression on the updated features can outperform a broad range of fixed kernels. The results show that one step can already provide substantial representational benefits under the analyzed conditions. They also identify learning-rate scaling as a key factor in whether early feature learning remains within a linear performance regime.
neurips-2022-high-dimensional-asymptotic.tldr: Under a proportional asymptotic model, one feature-learning step improves prediction, and sufficiently large steps can beat fixed kernels for certain targets.

paragraphs: A classifier usually learns both a feature-producing backbone and the final linear vectors that assign class scores. The paper questions whether those final vectors need to be learned. Its starting point is neural collapse: near the end of training on balanced data, class feature means and classifier vectors approach a highly symmetric geometric arrangement.

The authors initialize the classifier as a simplex equiangular tight frame and keep it fixed while learning features. This arrangement maximally separates the pairwise angles between classes. Analysis using a layer-peeled model indicates that feature learning with this fixed classifier leads to neural collapse even when classes have unequal numbers of training examples.

Within this setting, the authors also show that a simple squared loss can replace cross entropy while sharing its global optimality and offering better convergence properties. Experiments report significant improvements and faster convergence across multiple imbalanced datasets. Together, the analysis and results support using a prescribed classifier geometry to guide representation learning, with the theoretical conclusion tied to the model studied.
neurips-2022-inducing-neural-collapse-in.tldr: A fixed, geometrically symmetric classifier supports neural collapse under an analyzed imbalanced setting and improves empirical training results.

paragraphs: Few-shot semantic segmentation identifies target-object pixels in a query image using only a few annotated support images. A difficulty arises when objects from the same class look very different across support and query images. Information extracted from the support may then be a poor match for the object that must actually be segmented.

The proposed Intermediate Prototype Mining Transformer addresses this gap with a representation that draws information from both sides. The support supplies category information grounded in its annotations, while the query contributes information adapted to its own appearance. Each transformer layer updates this intermediate prototype using support and query features, then uses the prototype to activate the query feature map.

Repeating this exchange progressively refines both the prototype and the query representation before producing the segmentation. The authors report that the method substantially outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches on PASCAL-5i and COCO-20i. The findings support the value of adapting category information jointly with the query, especially for the support–query appearance differences that motivate the design.
neurips-2022-intermediate-prototype-mini.tldr: IPMT repeatedly combines support and query information into an intermediate prototype to improve few-shot segmentation.

paragraphs: Automated sellers can learn collusive pricing through reinforcement learning even without directly coordinating. Profit feedback alone can lead decentralized pricing algorithms toward prices that harm consumers. This paper examines whether the platform hosting those sellers can counter that behavior by changing how it promotes products and prices to shoppers.

The intervention is the buy box: the platform rules that determine which offers receive prominent placement. The authors use reinforcement learning to learn these rules, adopting a Stackelberg partially observable decision-process methodology. The resulting design problem concerns the platform’s promotion policy and its interaction with sellers that are themselves learning how to price.

The paper demonstrates that learned buy box rules can effectively prevent collusion by reinforcement-learning sellers in the studied settings. It also reports robustness when sellers use different behavior models or have goods costs outside the training distribution, while maintaining high consumer welfare. These results establish a promising use of platform-side learning to shape incentives and counter undesirable behavior emerging from seller-side learning.
neurips-2022-learning-to-mitigate-ai-col.tldr: Platforms can learn buy box rules that counter collusive reinforcement-learning sellers and sustain consumer welfare in tested settings.

paragraphs: Understanding long videos together with paragraphs requires tracking relationships across more time than short-clip pretraining typically addresses. More frames also increase computational demands. This paper introduces LF-VILA, a video-language model pretrained on a large collection of long videos and paragraphs constructed from an existing public dataset.

Two components address the temporal and computational challenges. A multimodal temporal contrastive loss encourages detailed alignment between videos and paragraphs so the model learns temporal relationships across the two modalities. A hierarchical temporal window attention mechanism captures long-range dependencies while reducing the transformer’s computational cost. Together, these components support efficient end-to-end learning from longer paired inputs.

After fine-tuning, LF-VILA achieves reported state-of-the-art performance on seven downstream tasks covering paragraph-to-video retrieval and long-form video question answering. The abstract reports relative improvements of 16.1% on ActivityNet paragraph-to-video retrieval and 2.4% on How2QA. These results support directly pretraining for long-form video-language understanding, with explicit mechanisms for both temporal alignment and efficient attention.
neurips-2022-long-form-video-language-pr.tldr: LF-VILA combines temporal video–text alignment with efficient attention to improve long-form retrieval and question answering.

paragraphs: Compressing a trained network reduces storage and computation, but matching its overall accuracy does not necessarily preserve its individual decisions. This paper targets compression that retains those decisions while maintaining network structure, selecting compression levels automatically, and working without fine-tuning. These goals make fidelity to the original model central to the compression process.

The method uses interpolative decompositions to select some channels or neurons and eliminate others. An interpolation matrix then carries a correction into the following layer, compensating for the removed components while preserving the network’s structure. The contribution combines component selection with an explicit adjustment to how the surviving representation is used.

A generalization bound for a one-layer network motivates a heuristic for choosing layer sizes in deeper networks. This distinguishes the directly analyzed case from the broader sizing procedure. Experiments span simple networks through deep ImageNet models and report strong performance, including good results without fine-tuning. The findings support compression that accounts for the original network’s behavior through structured corrections.
neurips-2022-model-preserving-compressio.tldr: Interpolative decompositions compress networks by removing channels and correcting subsequent layers, with good performance even without fine-tuning.

paragraphs: This paper treats trained neural networks themselves as a dataset. During training, a network’s weights and biases trace a trajectory through weight space. A population of networks therefore forms structures in that space, which the authors propose may reveal training progress and latent properties of individual models.

To make these questions easier to study systematically, the authors release diverse model populations generated with varying hyperparameter combinations. The collection spans eight image datasets and contains 27 model zoos. It includes 50,360 unique neural networks and their sparsified counterparts, with more than 3,844,360 collected model states representing the population across training.

The release also provides detailed analyses and benchmarks for multiple downstream tasks. These resources support research on model analysis, learning dynamics, representations of model populations, and potentially generating network weights and biases. The suggested information in weight-space geometry is a research motivation, while the concrete contribution is a standardized collection and evaluation foundation for investigating it.
neurips-2022-model-zoos-a-dataset-of-div.tldr: A dataset of diverse neural-network populations and training states supports systematic research on models as data.

paragraphs: The continuity equation expresses a fundamental conservation relationship between a density and its flow. This paper asks how to build neural representations that satisfy that relationship automatically. The goal is to encode conservation in the model’s construction, avoiding the need to enforce it through additional penalties or expensive numerical simulation.

The key observation is that solutions of the continuity equation can be expressed as divergence-free vector fields. The authors use differential forms to design neural networks with this property and implement two practical constructions with automatic differentiation. These networks parameterize density and vector-field pairs whose relationship satisfies the continuity equation by construction.

The paper also proves universality for the proposed models, establishing their ability to represent divergence-free vector fields rather than only a narrowly chosen family. Experiments validate the constructions through neural solutions of fluid equations, Hodge decomposition, and dynamical optimal transport maps. The contribution brings together an exact structural conservation property, expressive representation, and demonstrations across several related computational tasks.
neurips-2022-neural-conservation-laws-a-.tldr: Divergence-free neural constructions enforce the continuity equation by design and have a universality guarantee.

paragraphs: When a model serves several objectives, their gradients can point in conflicting directions. Methods such as PCGrad, MGDA, and CAGrad modify or combine gradients to reduce these conflicts. This paper examines a gap between their usual full-batch analysis and their practical use with noisy gradients estimated from mini-batches.

The authors express several methods within a unified framework in which weights determine how objective gradients form a combined update. An explicit convex problem with two objectives shows that stochastic versions may fail to converge to Pareto-optimal solutions. The analysis attributes this failure to choosing the combination weights solely from the current stochastic gradients.

The proposed repair exponentially averages previously calculated weights, making the combination depend on their history. The authors establish convergence of the resulting variant to Pareto-optimal or critical solutions and report comparable or improved empirical performance. The result identifies a specific failure mechanism and a corresponding modification; it does not claim that every use of stochastic gradient manipulation fails.
neurips-2022-on-the-convergence-of-stoch.tldr: Averaging gradient-combination weights over time repairs a demonstrated convergence failure in stochastic multi-objective optimization.

paragraphs: A predictor can express uncertainty by returning a set of plausible labels instead of committing to one label. This paper studies how to construct such prediction sets in meta-learning, where a model must adapt quickly to new tasks. The challenge is to retain a meaningful statistical guarantee when only a few examples are available for adaptation.

The authors introduce an algorithm for producing probably approximately correct, or PAC, prediction sets in this setting. Their guarantee extends the usual PAC formulation to account for future tasks: it holds with high probability over those tasks. This makes uncertainty across tasks part of the formal target, alongside adapting the predictor from limited task-specific data.

Experiments cover mini-ImageNet and CIFAR10-C for vision, FewRel for language, and the CDC Heart Dataset for medicine. The resulting sets satisfy the PAC guarantee while being smaller than those of comparison methods that also satisfy it. Smaller sets provide more selective outputs, so the reported advantage concerns informativeness while retaining the stated statistical protection.
neurips-2022-pac-prediction-sets-for-met.tldr: A meta-learning algorithm adapts compact prediction sets from few examples with PAC guarantees that extend across future tasks.

paragraphs: Pruning compresses a neural network by removing parts of it. Coreset approaches add theoretical control over how compression trades off against approximation error, but earlier methods depend on data or restrictive assumptions about weights and inputs. This paper develops a framework that requires only mild weight assumptions and makes no assumptions about the training data.

The method evaluates each neuron according to its importance for the output of the following layer. It combines Löwner ellipsoids and Carathéodory’s theorem to construct the relevant summaries. This geometric approach makes the pruning procedure data-independent while retaining theoretical support, broadening its applicability beyond the more restrictive coreset settings described by the authors.

Experiments report improvements over existing coreset-based pruning methods across varied networks and datasets. One example achieves a 62% compression rate for ResNet50 on ImageNet with a reported 1.09% drop in accuracy. The contribution is therefore a less restrictive framework with practical evidence behind it, while the remaining mild assumptions on weights still qualify its theoretical scope.
neurips-2022-pruning-neural-networks-via.tldr: A geometric coreset framework enables data-independent neural pruning with theoretical support under mild weight assumptions.

paragraphs: Pruning sometimes improves a network’s performance on unseen data, and a common explanation is that smaller models overfit less. This explanation becomes incomplete in over-parameterized regimes where larger models can generalize better. The paper empirically revisits why removing parameters can still improve generalization across a range of sparsities.

The authors find two distinct effects. At some sparsity levels, pruning produces better training, yielding lower training loss than the dense model. At other levels, it provides additional regularization, reducing the accuracy damage caused by noisy examples. These observations show why model size alone cannot fully explain the behavior of standard pruning procedures.

The paper connects better training to the additional training time introduced by pruning, and additional regularization to reduced model size. Its experiments indicate that both factors are needed to account fully for pruning’s observed generalization effects. The practical interpretation is that pruning changes the training process as well as the final network, and the dominant benefit can vary with sparsity.
neurips-2022-prunings-effect-on-generali.tldr: Empirical evidence links pruning’s generalization benefits to both additional training and the regularization from reduced model size.

paragraphs: Reducing video-frame resolution offers a route to cheaper recognition, but low-resolution inputs often produce poor accuracy. This paper investigates why that degradation occurs. Its central empirical finding is that the mismatch between network architecture and input scale is the main cause in the studied setting, rather than information lost during downsampling.

The authors introduce cross-resolution knowledge distillation, called ResKD, to bridge that mismatch. Knowledge transfer across resolutions helps the network recognize videos from smaller frames. This targets spatial input cost alongside more familiar efficiency strategies involving compact networks or reduced temporal redundancy.

ResKD reportedly surpasses competitive methods in both efficiency and accuracy on ActivityNet, FCVID, Mini-Kinetics, and Something-Something V2. The authors also demonstrate its effectiveness with 3D convolutional networks and video transformers, including very low-resolution inputs. These experiments support its potential as a broadly useful inference acceleration method. The explanation for accuracy loss remains an empirical finding from the paper’s study, rather than a claim that downsampling can never remove essential information.
neurips-2022-rethinking-resolution-in-th.tldr: Cross-resolution distillation improves low-resolution video recognition by addressing the observed mismatch between networks and input scale.

paragraphs: Pretraining on unlabeled data has improved many vision tasks, but it is less widely used for large three-dimensional scenes. This paper focuses on point clouds, including outdoor LiDAR data. Their distinctive structure means that pretraining frameworks developed for two-dimensional images do not readily transfer to these large 3D inputs.

The authors propose a self-supervised pretraining method specifically for large-scale 3D scenes. They apply it to commonly used point-based and voxel-based architectures, covering two ways of representing and processing the data. The learned representations are then transferred to 3D object detection and semantic segmentation, testing their usefulness for locating objects and assigning semantic categories.

The study demonstrates effectiveness on both dense indoor point clouds and sparse outdoor LiDAR point clouds. That coverage matters because the proposed pretraining is evaluated across substantially different scene and sampling characteristics. The main contribution is evidence that pretraining designed around large 3D data can benefit downstream understanding across both architectural families and both kinds of point-cloud environments.
neurips-2022-self-supervised-pretraining.tldr: Self-supervised pretraining tailored to large 3D point clouds benefits detection and segmentation across indoor and outdoor settings.

paragraphs: Regularization is commonly tuned to improve average performance on unseen examples. This paper shows that a setting selected across all classes can benefit the aggregate result while severely harming particular categories. It examines both data augmentation and weight decay, finding that their effects on model complexity are uneven across classes.

One reported example concerns an ImageNet ResNet50: introducing random-crop augmentation reduces barn-spider test accuracy from 68% to 46%. Class-specific drops also appear with weight decay, so the issue extends beyond the content changes introduced by image transformations. The findings challenge the idea that a globally preferred regularization strength is equally suitable for each class.

The consequences also carry into transfer learning. In a reported INaturalist example, random cropping during ImageNet pretraining reduces accuracy on class #8889 from 70% to 30%. The paper argues that average generalization metrics can conceal substantial class-level losses. It leaves identifying a measure of model complexity without class-dependent preference as an open research question.
neurips-2022-the-effects-of-regularizati.tldr: Regularization selected for average accuracy can substantially damage individual classes, including after transfer to another dataset.

paragraphs: Cake cutting studies how to divide a resource fairly when participants value its parts differently. This paper asks how many queries about those preferences are needed to compute approximate fair allocations. It considers envy-free, perfect, and equitable allocations while also requiring the minimum number of cuts.

The authors establish upper and lower bounds, separating what algorithms can achieve from what any algorithm must spend in the query model. Tight bounds are obtained for contiguous envy-free allocations with three players, and for perfect and equitable allocations with minimum cuts between two players. For contiguous ε-envy-free allocations with any n ≥ 3, they give an O(n/ε) upper bound and an Ω(log(1/ε)) lower bound.

The paper also formalizes moving-knife procedures, which describe allocation through continuously moving cuts. It shows that a large subclass containing all known procedures can be simulated efficiently with arbitrarily small error in the Robertson–Webb query model. This connects continuous descriptions of fair-division procedures to algorithms that obtain information through discrete queries.
neurips-2022-the-query-complexity-of-cak.tldr: The paper bounds the preference queries needed for approximate fair division and efficiently simulates a broad class of moving-knife procedures.

paragraphs: Sounding-object localization identifies the object in a scene that produces a specified sound. Accurate bounding-box annotations are scarce for this task, despite the availability of substantial training data. This paper investigates whether knowledge from related tasks can supply the localization capability without using data from the target field.

The proposed Two-stream Universal Referring localization Network, or TURN, separates two functions. A localization stream acquires object-localization knowledge from image grounding, while an alignment stream learns a semantic space shared by text and audio. This shared representation allows knowledge associated with textual references to be connected to sound inputs.

An adaptive sampling strategy identifies overlap between the different data domains, improving performance and stability. Experiments on public benchmarks show competitive results relative to state-of-the-art approaches without training on data from the sounding-object-localization field. The findings support the feasibility of transferring localization knowledge through aligned modalities: the zero-resource claim concerns the target field, while the method deliberately draws on related tasks and data.
neurips-2022-towards-effective-multi-mod.tldr: TURN transfers image-grounding knowledge through text–audio alignment to localize sounding objects without target-field training data.

paragraphs: A shape program describes an object by composing reusable part routines. Reusing a routine for repeated parts captures relationships such as geometric similarity and symmetry. Earlier learning-based approaches have been constrained by coarse part representations and by the need for expensive, manually annotated programs to supervise training.

ProGRIP represents parts with implicit functions, increasing the geometric detail that the program can express while preserving its higher-level organization around repetition and symmetry. The authors also introduce a matching-based unsupervised training objective. This removes the requirement for ground-truth program annotations, addressing the supervision burden alongside the representation limitation.

Empirical studies show better shape reconstruction fidelity and more accurate semantic-part segmentation than existing structured representations. These outcomes evaluate both the reconstructed object and its organization into meaningful parts. The contribution is a combination of richer part geometry and reusable program structure, learned without annotated programs, with reported benefits for both reconstructing shapes and identifying their semantic components.
neurips-2022-unsupervised-learning-of-sh.tldr: ProGRIP learns reusable shape programs with detailed implicit parts without program annotations, improving reconstruction and part segmentation.

paragraphs: Vision transformers can perform well without explicitly building spatial locality into their architecture. This paper asks how gradient-based training from random initialization can nevertheless recover spatial patterns. To investigate, the authors construct a structured classification dataset and analyze a simplified transformer rather than attempting a theory of every component in a full vision transformer.

Their positional attention mechanism makes the attention matrix depend only on positional encodings. Although the classification problem has multiple generalizing solutions, the analyzed model implicitly learns the dataset’s spatial structure while generalizing. The authors also prove that this learned structure supports sample-efficient transfer when downstream datasets share the structure but use different features.

Experiments show that transformers using positional attention alone perform similarly to original vision transformers on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, and ImageNet. These results complement the theoretical analysis by examining the simplified mechanism on established image tasks. The paper offers preliminary theoretical justification for spatial structure learning, with its formal transfer result specifically requiring shared structure between pretraining and downstream data.
neurips-2022-vision-transformers-provabl.tldr: A simplified vision transformer provably learns spatial structure that improves transfer to datasets sharing that structure.
